title: Establishing CFD model credibility of a centrifugal blood pump for hemolysis and shear exposure: A multi-mechanism ASME V&V 40 assessment
device: Centrifugal blood pump intended for circulatory support

models.name: Model A: Steady RANS Pump Flow Solver (k-ω SST)
models.what_it_computes: Time-averaged 3D velocity, pressure, viscous shear rate, and wall shear distributions throughout the rotating assembly and volute under specified operating points.

models.name: Model B: Eulerian Hemolysis Scalar Transport
models.what_it_computes: An advected hemolysis index field driven by local shear exposure and residence time, yielding volumetric hemoglobin release rate and outlet-averaged hemolysis metrics.

models.name: Model C: Lagrangian Particle Damage Accumulation
models.what_it_computes: Trajectory-resolved residence times and cumulative red-blood-cell damage along pathlines, producing distributions of exposure dose and hotspot identification.

mechanisms.name: M1: Boundary-layer shear on blades and shroud
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Sustained near-wall viscous shear contributes to sublethal and lethal red-cell damage as fluid glides along rotating and stationary surfaces.

mechanisms.name: M2: Tip-leakage and rotor–stator interaction peaks
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Localized high-shear transients in the gap and wake regions generate short-duration but intense stresses implicated in hemolysis bursts.

mechanisms.name: M3: Recirculation-driven residence time in the volute
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Slow-moving zones extend cumulative exposure, amplifying damage even at moderate shear and elevating outlet plasma-free hemoglobin.

clear_factors: Relevance of the quantities of interest
Relevance of the validation activities to the COU

deviation.detail: All credibility factors are scored per model–mechanism on a 0–4 scale (0=not met, 1=limited, 2=adequate, 3=strong, 4=compelling) and summarized numerically.

sections: Question of Interest and Context of Use: Decision support for predicting pump hemolysis and shear exposure across 2–5 L/min and 80–120 mmHg. COU: Use the three CFD models to estimate outlet hemolysis rate, 99th-percentile accumulated shear exposure, and volume exceeding critical shear–time thresholds to inform design verification without additional bench testing at all operating points. Model Risk Level: High. Rationale: Model influence is high because CFD outputs are the primary evidence to accept operating ranges; decision consequence is high because underpredicted hemolysis can lead to clinically significant adverse events.
Computational Models: Governing equations, numerical schemes, and coupling among Model A, Model B, and Model C
Hemolysis-Relevant Mechanisms: Definitions of M1 boundary-layer shear, M2 tip-leakage peaks, and M3 recirculation-residence phenomena
Quantities of Interest and Their Relevance: Outlet hemolysis rate, exposure percentiles, and critical-shear volume fractions tied to clinical and bench readouts
Model Inputs: Operating map, fluid rheology, red-cell properties, and hemolysis model coefficients
Equivalency of Input Parameters: Alignment of CFD boundary conditions, hematocrit, temperature, and viscosity with validation tests by operating point
Software Quality Assurance: Solver version control, automated regression tests, and case management for Models A–C
Validation Activities and Relevance to the COU: In-vitro loop measurements of plasma-free hemoglobin and laser-Doppler velocimetry mapped to M1–M3 operating envelopes
Test Samples: Pump hardware lots, blood analog and anticoagulated blood preparations, and sampling cadence for hemolysis assays
Credibility Scoring Method: Factor-by-factor ratings on the 0–4 scale for each model–mechanism pair; aggregation and visualization plan
Results: Credibility factor scores for each (Model A–C) × (M1–M3) combination on the 0–4 scale, with narrative support
Discussion: Interpretation of factor scores limited to the seven assessed factors; implications for the COU
Considerations Related to Use Error: Brief observations on speed setpoint handling and priming practices in relation to modeled operating points
